# Free Constitution

> Know your rights. In plain English.

freeconstitution.org is a free plain-English guide to the United States Constitution, published by Hope for Americans (Flagstaff, Arizona). No ads, no tracking, no accounts.

## Content policy
- Original text of the Constitution, all 27 amendments, and the Declaration of Independence comes from the National Archives (public domain).
- Plain-language explanations and situation cards are original work by Hope for Americans, licensed CC BY 4.0.
- Legal claims are checked against the text and named Supreme Court decisions. The site has not been reviewed by a lawyer and is not legal advice.

## Amendments
- [First Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/1/): The government cannot punish you for your religion, your speech, what you publish, peaceful protest, or asking officials to fix things.
- [Second Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/2/): The Supreme Court says you have an individual right to keep and carry guns, but governments can still pass some gun laws.
- [Third Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/3/): In peacetime, the government cannot make you house soldiers in your home without your consent.
- [Fourth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/4/): Police generally need a warrant, your consent, or a legal exception to search you, your home, your phone, or your things.
- [Fifth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/5/): You can't be forced to testify against yourself or tried twice for the same crime, and the government must treat you fairly.
- [Sixth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/6/): If you're charged with a crime, you have the right to a lawyer, a fair jury, a speedy public trial, and to question witnesses.
- [Seventh Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/7/): In most federal civil lawsuits, you have the right to have a jury decide the facts.
- [Eighth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/8/): The government cannot set bail or fines that are too high, or use cruel and unusual punishments.
- [Ninth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/9/): The Constitution lists some of your rights, but not all of them. You keep rights that are not on the list.
- [Tenth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/10/): The federal government has only the powers the Constitution gives it. Other powers belong to the states or to the people.
- [Eleventh Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/11/): A state generally cannot be sued in federal court without its consent. This rule is called sovereign immunity.
- [Twelfth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/12/): Electors cast separate votes for President and Vice President. If no one wins a majority, Congress makes the choice.
- [Thirteenth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/13/): Slavery and forced labor are banned everywhere in the United States, except as punishment for someone convicted of a crime.
- [Fourteenth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/14/): Almost everyone born here is a citizen, and states must give every person fair legal process and equal treatment under the law.
- [Fifteenth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/15/): No government can deny or limit your right to vote because of your race or color.
- [Sixteenth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/16/): Congress can tax your income, from any source, without dividing the tax among the states by population.
- [Seventeenth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/17/): Voters in each state elect their two U.S. senators directly. Before 1913, state lawmakers chose them.
- [Eighteenth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/18/): This amendment banned making, selling, and transporting alcohol nationwide starting in 1920. It was repealed in 1933.
- [Nineteenth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/19/): No government can deny or limit your right to vote because of your sex.
- [Twentieth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/20/): New Presidents start on January 20, and new members of Congress start on January 3, after the November election.
- [Twenty-first Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/21/): This amendment ended national Prohibition in 1933 and lets each state make its own alcohol laws.
- [Twenty-second Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/22/): No one can be elected President more than twice.
- [Twenty-third Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/23/): People who live in Washington, D.C., can vote for President. D.C. gets 3 electoral votes, the same as the smallest states.
- [Twenty-fourth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/24/): No one can be charged a fee to vote in a federal election. A 1966 Supreme Court ruling extended this to state elections.
- [Twenty-fifth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/25/): If the President dies, resigns, or cannot do the job, the Vice President takes over, sometimes for only a few hours.
- [Twenty-sixth Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/26/): If you are a U.S. citizen and 18 or older, no government can stop you from voting because of your age.
- [Twenty-seventh Amendment](https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/27/): If Congress votes to change its own pay, the change cannot start until after the next House election.

## Situation cards
- [Being questioned by police](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/being-questioned-by-police/): What to say and do if police are asking you questions on the street, in a car, or at a station.
- [Searched by police](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/searched-by-police/): What to say and do if police want to search you, your bag, your car, your phone, or your home.
- [At school](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/at-school/): Your rights at a public school when staff want to search you, question you, or punish you for something you said.
- [Posting online](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/posting-online/): What the First Amendment does and does not protect when you post online, and who it limits.
- [At work](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/at-work/): Which rights you have at work, why the Constitution mostly does not limit private employers, and which laws may help.
- [Recording police](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/recording-police/): What courts have said about recording police in public, how to do it without interfering, and what police can do with your phone.
- [First-time voter](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/first-time-voter/): How to register, what ID you may need, and your rights at the polls when you vote for the first time.
- [At a protest](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/at-a-protest/): What to say and do if you are stopped, questioned, or threatened with arrest at a protest.
- [Turned away from voting](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/turned-away-from-voting/): What to do if a poll worker says you cannot vote, your name is not on the list, or you lack the right ID.
- [Immigration agents at the door](https://freeconstitution.org/situations/immigration-agents-at-the-door/): What to say and do if immigration agents knock on your door, whatever your immigration status.
